options.text: Bundling state with the operations on that state, and restricting external access to the representation
Deriving a new class from an existing one to reuse its code
Allowing one interface to be satisfied by many implementations
Declaring every field `private` and generating a getter and setter for each

questions.explanation: Encapsulation combines two ideas: the object owns both its data and the operations that maintain it, and the representation is reachable only through a published interface. That boundary is what lets the class enforce its invariants, because no external code can put the object into an inconsistent state.

distractorRationale.d: A public getter and setter for every private field re-exposes the representation, so it provides the syntax of encapsulation with none of the benefit

questions.stem: With **dynamic dispatch**, which implementation of an overridden method is invoked by a call?

options.text: The one in the declared (static) type of the reference
The one in the actual (run-time) class of the receiving object
The one in the root of the class hierarchy
The one in whichever class textually appears last in the source file

questions.explanation: Dynamic dispatch resolves an overridden method against the object's run-time class, typically by an indirect jump through a virtual method table stored with the object. This is exactly what makes subtype polymorphism useful: the caller writes against the supertype and each subtype supplies its own behaviour.

distractorRationale.a: The static type determines only which methods are *visible* to the compiler, not which body runs
distractorRationale.c: The root implementation runs only when no subclass overrides it
distractorRationale.d: Source order has no bearing on dispatch

questions.stem: A `Course` needs the behaviour of a `Timetable` in order to publish its schedule, but a course is not a kind of timetable. Which design is appropriate?

options.text: `Course` extends `Timetable`, inheriting its methods
`Course` holds a `Timetable` as a field and delegates to it
`Timetable` extends `Course`, so courses gain scheduling
Both classes extend a common abstract `Schedulable` base to share the code

questions.explanation: Inheritance expresses an **is-a** relationship and should be used only where a subclass is substitutable for its supertype everywhere. Here the relationship is **has-a**, so composition with delegation is correct: `Course` keeps a `Timetable` field and forwards the scheduling calls. This also keeps `Timetable` replaceable without touching `Course`'s own interface.

distractorRationale.a: Inheriting purely to reuse code creates a false is-a claim and exposes every `Timetable` method on `Course`'s interface
distractorRationale.c: Inverts the dependency and is an even weaker is-a claim
distractorRationale.d: Introducing a shared base to reuse an implementation is inheritance-for-reuse again; a common base is justified only when both genuinely are subtypes of it

questions.stem:
What is printed?

`class A { describe() { print("code=" + this.tag()) }  tag() { return "A" } }`
`class B extends A { tag() { return "B" } }`
`A obj = new B(); obj.describe();`

options.text: `code=A`
`code=B`
`code=AB`
A compile error, because `B` does not define `describe`

questions.explanation: `describe` is inherited from `A`, so the body executing is `A`'s. But the call `this.tag()` inside it is itself dynamically dispatched on the run-time class of the receiver, which is `B`, so `B.tag()` runs. This is the *template method* mechanism: a fixed algorithm in the base class calling overridable steps in the subclass.

distractorRationale.a: Assumes that because the executing body lives in `A`, the nested call is resolved statically in `A` too
distractorRationale.c: Assumes both implementations run and are concatenated; overriding replaces rather than appends
distractorRationale.d: `B` inherits `describe` from `A`, so the call type-checks

questions.stem: In a language with single implementation inheritance but multiple interface implementation, what is the principal advantage of declaring a pure **interface** rather than an abstract class?

options.text: Interfaces are dispatched faster because they hold no state
A class may implement many interfaces but extend only one class, so interfaces compose without constraining the hierarchy
Interfaces can declare fields, whereas abstract classes cannot
Interfaces are checked at run time only, so they impose no compile-time cost

questions.explanation: An interface specifies a capability without consuming the single inheritance slot, so a class can be `Comparable`, `Serializable` and `Printable` at once. An abstract class is the right choice when you must share state or a partial implementation among subtypes, which an interface cannot do.

distractorRationale.a: Interface dispatch typically costs the same as or slightly more than class virtual dispatch, since the target may need a lookup in an interface method table
distractorRationale.c: The reverse is true: abstract classes may declare instance fields, interfaces generally may not
distractorRationale.d: Interface conformance is a compile-time check in statically typed languages

questions.stem: `Rectangle` has independent `setWidth` and `setHeight`. `Square extends Rectangle` and overrides both so that setting either dimension sets both. Why is this a design defect?

options.text: It violates the Liskov substitution principle: code relying on `Rectangle`'s postcondition that setting width leaves height unchanged breaks when handed a `Square`
It violates encapsulation, because `Square` accesses the fields of `Rectangle`
It is invalid because a subclass may not override more than one inherited method
It causes infinite recursion between the two setters

questions.explanation: Substitutability is a statement about behaviour, not just signatures. `Rectangle` promises that `setWidth(5)` leaves the height alone; `Square` cannot honour that promise, so a `Square` is not a behavioural subtype however natural the geometric "is-a" sounds. The standard remedies are to make the shapes immutable, so no setter exists to contradict, or to drop the inheritance relationship entirely.

distractorRationale.b: A subclass legitimately accessing protected state is not the problem here
distractorRationale.c: There is no such rule; overriding several methods is routine
distractorRationale.d: A correct implementation assigns the fields directly and does not recurse

questions.stem: `class Base { void f(Object o) { print("Base-Object") } }` and `class Derived extends Base { void f(String s) { print("Derived-String") } }`. Given `Base b = new Derived();` what does `b.f("hello")` print?

options.text: `Base-Object`
`Derived-String`
Both lines, in declaration order
A compile error, because `Derived` does not override `f(Object)`

questions.explanation: Two separate resolutions happen. **Overload resolution** is static: the compiler sees only the static type `Base`, whose sole applicable method is `f(Object)`, so it fixes that signature. **Override resolution** is then dynamic, but `Derived` does not override `f(Object)` — `f(String)` is an unrelated overload — so `Base`'s body runs. Overloading is chosen at compile time, overriding at run time; conflating the two produces exactly this error.

distractorRationale.b: Assumes the more specific overload in the run-time class is selected, which would require overload resolution to be dynamic
distractorRationale.c: Only one method body is invoked per call
distractorRationale.d: No override is required; `Derived` inherits `f(Object)` and simply adds an overload

questions.stem: A class whose every private field has a public getter and a public setter is well encapsulated.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. A getter and setter for every field publishes the representation under a slightly longer name; callers still depend on the exact field set, and the class still cannot enforce any invariant that spans two fields. Real encapsulation means exposing operations expressed in the domain — `withdraw(amount)` rather than `setBalance(...)` — so the class remains the sole enforcer of its invariants.
